posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
Let me approach this from a different perspective that might make it easier to understand. Before we even start talking about jack handle, let’s go through the basic order of operations when you deal damage:

 

1) Determine attack type type (not relevant to this conversation.

2) Determine base attack (the number listed on the card that is dealing the damage).

3) Determine all modifiers, you can choose the order.

4) If the number is greater than 0, reduce hp by that amount (obviously, not if they are immune).

 

Let’s focus on step #3. In this step you take all modifiers into account: plus/minus of the attacker, and plus/minus of the defender. You can choose the order that all of these modifiers come into effect. For example, if the target has -1 damage reduction, and the attacker has +1 damage, you can either do +1 - 1 or -1 + 1. There will be many times will it simply will not matter, but sometimes it can. The point is that all modifiers are assessed at the same time.

 

Using this basic order of operations that is used in every situation in SotM, we can understand how Jack Handles work. There are essentially three options:

 

A) Only taking some modifiers into account:

 

1) Determine attack type.

2) Determine base damage.

3) Determine all modifiers that only apply to the attacker.

4) Calculate this damage and apply it to all non-villain targets

5) For each target, determine their modifiers (it makes no sense to ignore these modifiers and actually deal damage based on step #4).

6) If the number is greater than 0, reduce hp (if not immune).

 

I really don’t see how the card can drastically affect the order of operations, there is nothing in the card itself that says you only take certain modifiers into account first, then others later. To say this would be a big stretch.

 

B) Determine all modifiers, then change source:

 

1) Determine attack type type.

2) Determine base attack (the number listed on the card that is dealing the damage).

3) Determine all modifiers, you can choose the order.

4) If the number is greater than 0, ignore this attack, and deal that same hp that would be loss to all non-villain targets, modified for the individual targets.

 

In theory, this might be a good interpretation, except that we have a ruling that says it isn’t. If this was the way everything was handled, then Fixer could hit himself with Bloody Knuckles to deal everyone else 5 damage, but we know that he can’t. So, this one is out too.

 

C) Determine only base damage:

 

1) Determine attack type.

2) Determine base damage.

3) Calculate base damage and apply it to all non-villain targets.

4) Determine all modifiers for each target, you can choose the order.

5) If the number is greater than 0, reduce hp by that amount for each target (obviously, not if they are immune).

 

Essentially, by necessity, this is the only interpretation that fits. If so, only the first target would get the bonus damage.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
Jack Handle is not an X damage card.  The initial damage isn't dealt, the process alters it to instead hit all non-hero targets.

That step comes first, before you calculate modifiers to damage.

For example Twist the Ether affects Jack handle by each individual instance of damage, not treating it as one instance.  In the same way Galvanize will increase each instance individually, and Critical Multiplier will work the same, treating each instance as a seperate instance of damage, and thus only affecting the first instance.

It works the same as Crowbars, turning the initial deal 1 target 1 damage into deal 2 targets 1 damage.  It then increases both by 1.

 

Absolute Zero works differently because he takes damage, and then responds with X damage.

 

For Jack Handle to work the way people are saying it does it would be worded:  

When Mr. Fixer deals damage, deal each other non-hero target X damage of the same type, where X is the amount of damage Mr. Fixer dealt.

Sorry if I'm just repeating something that's already been said/discussed, but the way I see it, there's one of two ways this combo works.

1) Mr. Fixer is about to deal damage to a target. Jack Handle then says "This is actually going to happen to everyone." So no damage is dealt before a single target instance turns into an AoE. This means you would apply the first instance in order, from target to target. So if you're about to damage a Gene-Bound target, Jack Handle kicks in. Then for each instance of damage, you apply the modifiers. For the first instance, you deal 1+x, where X = "additional modifiers the first time you deal damage."  Because damage is never simultaneous, you would break the combat down into instances.

2) You take the card more literally, and determine the first instance of damage, and then go on to apply the same amount of damage for everything else. This more closely follows the damage dealing order of operations. So first you apply the modifiers to his initial "strike" power. Let's say he does +3 damage for a total of 4. Next we confirm that he is in fact dealing damage; Jack Handle kicks in. Jack Handle then says "okay, we're doing this damage to everything now." So everything takes 4.

I'm leaning toward #2. The way Jack Handle is worded, it copies the first damage instance (which would still technically be the first target being hit) and applies it to all targets. Or does the game remove modifiers after moving on to check if damage is being dealt somehow?

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
Not entirely sure what you mean, but I don't think who you targeted should matter. Mr. Fixer is great against The Rat, because all of that self damage and damage to other heroes gets redirected to The Rat (cancel that first attack, then hit all non-hero targets). If it mattered who you hit, that would never work. If you say that the "next damage" buff should apply to every target, then so should Bloody Knuckles. Mr. Fixer hits himself with Bloody Knuckles in play, base attack 1 damage, +2 for Bloody Knuckles, then another +2 for Bloody Knuckles. Now, that same damge should then apply to all other targets as the final damage modifications, but it isn't.

Let's go through how it would work if the "next damage" buff would work.

1) Mr. Fixer targets something.

2) Add in all modifications from the attacker and defender.

3) Determine if hp was reduced.

4) If no hp was reduced, then no damage would have been dealt, and it doesn't then hit all non-hero targets. If an hp was reduced, then we can hit all non-hero targets.

We have this strange word of "that" and there are two methods to go to from here:

A) We reevaluate all modifications, and start fresh with new targets (just like redirections). In this case, only the first one hit will get the buff.

B) We only take some of the modifications. Because of the Bloody Knuckles ruling, we know that damage modifications from the defender do not matter. So, even though we needed to calculate the modifications to see if any hp was reduced in order to see if we can hit other targets, we are now going to ignore those modifications, but keep others. Honestly, this is a stretch, and if true, the word "that" is one amazing word. It doesn't actually mean "that whole damage," but only "some of that damage."
